claim: The anaphase B spindle in fission yeast has a slender morphology and must elongate against compressive forces.
source: The anaphase B spindle in fission yeast has a slender morphology and must elongate against compressive forces.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by references to spindle severance experiments in the introduction.

claim: The 'pushing' mode of chromosome transport renders the spindle susceptible to breakage, as observed in cells with a variety of defects.
source: This 'pushing' mode of chromosome transport renders the spindle susceptible to breakage, as observed in cells with a variety of defects.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to studies showing spindle breakage in cells with defects.

claim: The spindle organizes microtubules into a rigid transverse array to maintain structural integrity.
source: Structural integrity is maintained throughout the spindle's fourfold elongation by organising microtubules into a rigid transverse array, preserving correct microtubule number and dynamically rescaling microtubule length.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by electron tomography data showing crystalline microtubule arrangements.

claim: The rate of elongation and timing of each mitotic stage are highly consistent in different fission yeast cells.
source: The first advantage of studying mitosis in Schizosaccharomyces pombe is that the rate of elongation and the timing of each mitotic stage are highly consistent in different cells (Mallavarapu et al., 1999; Fu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Anaphase B spindle elongation is driven by outward sliding of overlapping microtubules by plus-end directed molecular motors located at its centre.
source: A second advantage is that anaphase B spindle elongation represents a clearly defined morphogenetic transition that is driven by outward sliding of overlapping microtubules by plus-end directed molecular motors located at its centre (Tolić-Nørrelykke, Sacconi, et al., 2004b; Khodjakov et al., 2004; Fu et al., 2009; Glotzer, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple supporting citations.

claim: Microtubule minus-ends are static and remain anchored at the spindle pole body.
source: Microtubule minus-ends are static and remain anchored at the spindle pole body, whilst growth of inter-polar microtubules at their plus-ends is coordinated with outward sliding to maintain an overlap at the spindle centre (Mallavarapu et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Spindle elongation is powered by internal forces and resisted by external compressive loads.
source: Spindle severance experiments have revealed that spindle elongation is powered by internal forces, and resisted by external compressive loads (Tolić-Nørrelykke, Sacconi, et al., 2004b; Khodjakov et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations to spindle severance experiments.

claim: Buckling of the spindle followed by its breakage is a common failure mode for cells with defects in chromosome condensation, the nuclear envelope, or spindle microtubule organization.
source: These external loads can compromise the fidelity of chromosome segregation, as it has been observed that buckling of the spindle followed by its breakage is a common failure mode for cells that have defects in chromosome condensation, the nuclear envelope or in the organisation of spindle microtubules (Courtheoux et al., 2009; Khmelinskii et al., 2009; Yam et al., 2011; Petrova et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple supporting citations.

claim: The spindle is composed of two opposing arrays of pole-nucleated microtubules that interdigitate at the spindle midzone.
source: Our ET reconstructions confirmed that the spindle is composed of two opposing arrays of pole-nucleated microtubules that interdigitate at the spindle midzone (Figure 1B; Videos 3–5).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by electron tomography reconstructions shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A similar gross spindle organisation was observed in previous serial-section reconstructions of cdc25.22 fission yeast cells and budding yeast spindles.
source: A similar gross spindle organisation was observed in previous serial-section reconstructions of cdc25.22 fission yeast cells (Ding et al., 1993) and the related budding yeast spindle (Winey et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations to previous studies.

claim: Microtubules at the spindle midzone form arrays with a degree of square-packed order from late metaphase onwards.
source: A visualisation of the IFTA results (Figure 1C) reveals that microtubules at the spindle midzone form arrays with a degree of square-packed order from late metaphase onwards.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by IFTA analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: All anaphase B spindles contain at least four microtubules arranged as the vertices of a square at the midzone.
source: We frequently observe square arrays containing a 3 × 3 'checkerboard' arrangement of microtubules at the midzone of spindles from the end of metaphase and early in anaphase B, whilst all of the later spindles contain at least four microtubules arranged as the vertices of a square.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on observations from electron tomography.

claim: The polar regions of the spindle are loosely packed in metaphase but become more tightly packed in anaphase B.
source: The polar regions of the spindle are loosely packed in metaphase but become more tightly packed in anaphase B, where we observe three microtubules arranged in an equilateral triangle motif in all of the reconstructed spindles.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on electron tomography observations.

claim: Thin filaments of electron density that bridge the spaces between microtubules are present at both the midzone and the flanking regions.
source: An inspection of the raw tomographic images (Figure 1D) reveals good agreement with the results of IFTA, and also shows that thin filaments of electron density that bridge the spaces between microtubules are present at both the midzone and the flanking regions.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by raw tomographic images in Figure 1D.

claim: In metaphase, the microtubule overlap spans across the spindle.
source: An analysis of the lengths of microtubules with respect to the spindle's contour length (Figure 1C) shows that the microtubule overlap spans across the spindle in metaphase.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In anaphase B, the midzone occupies the central portion of the spindle with a symmetric width of around 2 μm.
source: In anaphase B, the midzone occupies the central portion of the spindle with a symmetric width of around 2 μm.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on analysis of microtubule lengths.

claim: The spindle midzone has square-packed character (θ ∼ 90°) with a large spanning distance (d ∼ 40 nm).
source: Statistical analyses of IFTA results from anaphase B spindles (Figure 1E) confirm the square-packed character (θ ∼ 90°) with a large spanning distance (d ∼ 40 nm) at the spindle midzone.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The regions flanking the midzone have denser packing (d ∼ 30 nm) with hexagonal character (θ ∼ 60°).
source: Conversely, denser packing (d ∼ 30 nm) with hexagonal character (θ ∼ 60°) is present in the regions that flank the midzone (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Square packing at the midzone suggests that microtubules are bundled in an anti-parallel orientation.
source: The square packing suggests that the microtubules are bundled in an anti-parallel orientation at the spindle midzone (Ding et al., 1993; Janson et al., 2007);
evidence: This is stated in the results with supporting citations.

claim: Hexagonal packing in the regions closer to the spindle poles is indicative of microtubules being bundled in parallel.
source: whilst hexagonal packing in the regions closer to the spindle poles is indicative of microtubules being bundled in parallel (McDonald et al., 1979).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: The spindle contains around thirty microtubules during metaphase.
source: The ET shows that the spindle contains around thirty microtubules during metaphase, and that this number is reduced dramatically by kinetochore-fibre depolymerisation in anaphase A (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Upon entry into anaphase B, the spindle is constructed from only ten microtubules.
source: Upon entry into anaphase B, the spindle is constructed from only ten microtubules, which are then lost progressively from the spindle until only six remain prior to its disassembly.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on electron tomography data.

claim: The total microtubule length polymerised within the spindle peaks at around 30 μm at the end of metaphase.
source: Concomitant with the changes in microtubule number, the total microtubule length polymerised within the spindle peaks at around 30 μm at the end of metaphase, but then remains roughly constant in anaphase B as the spindle length increases by a factor of four (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The total microtubule length remains roughly constant in anaphase B as the spindle length increases by a factor of four.
source: Concomitant with the changes in microtubule number, the total microtubule length polymerised within the spindle peaks at around 30 μm at the end of metaphase, but then remains roughly constant in anaphase B as the spindle length increases by a factor of four (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Live-cell imaging confirmed that the intensity of GFP-labelled tubulin incorporated into the spindle plateaus shortly after the metaphase-to-anaphase transition.
source: This result was confirmed by live-cell imaging, which indicated that the intensity of the GFP-labelled tubulin incorporated into the spindle also plateaus shortly after the metaphase-to-anaphase transition (Figure 1H; Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 1H and supplementary figures.

claim: The tubulin concentration in fission yeast is 4.3 ± 0.8 μM.
source: This technique yields an estimate for the tubulin concentration (4.3 ± 0.8 μM) that is a factor of five lower than in metazoan cells (Gard and Kirschner, 1987), and is in good agreement with mass spectrometry estimates of the abundance of tubulin isoforms (Marguerat et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by calibration of fluorescent intensity to ET data, with comparison to mass spectrometry.

claim: The tubulin concentration in fission yeast is a factor of five lower than in metazoan cells.
source: This technique yields an estimate for the tubulin concentration (4.3 ± 0.8 μM) that is a factor of five lower than in metazoan cells (Gard and Kirschner, 1987), and is in good agreement with mass spectrometry estimates of the abundance of tubulin isoforms (Marguerat et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a citation to metazoan cell measurements.

claim: All microtubule dynamics occur at the plus-tips of spindle microtubules during anaphase B.
source: Since all microtubule dynamics occur at the plus-tips of spindle microtubules during anaphase B (Mallavarapu et al., 1999), the conservation of polymer mass suggests that microtubule depolymerisation and recycling of tubulin subunits into the free pool (Walker et al., 1988) may be required for growth of the surviving interpolar microtubules, as suggested by previous EM reconstructions of fission yeast cells containing the cdc25.22 mutation (Ding et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated in the results with supporting citations.

claim: Microtubule depolymerisation and recycling of tubulin subunits may be required for growth of the surviving interpolar microtubules.
source: Since all microtubule dynamics occur at the plus-tips of spindle microtubules during anaphase B (Mallavarapu et al., 1999), the conservation of polymer mass suggests that microtubule depolymerisation and recycling of tubulin subunits into the free pool (Walker et al., 1988) may be required for growth of the surviving interpolar microtubules, as suggested by previous EM reconstructions of fission yeast cells containing the cdc25.22 mutation (Ding et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated in the results as a suggestion based on polymer mass conservation and previous studies.

claim: Cells from the cdc25.22 genetic background are enlarged upon entry into mitosis.
source: Interestingly, cells from the cdc25.22 genetic background are enlarged upon entry into mitosis (West et al., 2001), and can be compared with the wild-type spindle to provide insight into how the spindle's architecture is altered by increases in cytoplasmic volume.
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: The increased quantity of polymerised tubulin in cdc25.22 mutant cells arises from the increased cytoplasmic volume and the corresponding twofold increase in the abundance of tubulin and other spindle assembly factors.
source: This suggests that the increased quantity of polymerised tubulin in cdc25.22 mutant cells arises from the increased cytoplasmic volume and the corresponding twofold increase in the abundance of tubulin and other spindle assembly factors.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a suggestion based on comparison of wild-type and cdc25.22 cells.

claim: In wild-type cells, the square-packed organisation with a regular 40 nm centre-to-centre microtubule separation is established during metaphase.
source: In particular, we have observed that, in wild-type cells, the square-packed organisation with a regular 40 nm centre-to-centre microtubule separation is established during metaphase whereas spindles from the same stage in the cdc25.22 mutants appear to have a less ordered midzone architecture (Ding et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on observations from electron tomography.

claim: Spindles from metaphase in cdc25.22 mutants appear to have a less ordered midzone architecture.
source: In particular, we have observed that, in wild-type cells, the square-packed organisation with a regular 40 nm centre-to-centre microtubule separation is established during metaphase whereas spindles from the same stage in the cdc25.22 mutants appear to have a less ordered midzone architecture (Ding et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a citation to previous work.

claim: Square packing is present at the midzone of anaphase B spindles in both wild-type and cdc25.22 genetic backgrounds.
source: Square packing is present at the midzone of anaphase B spindles in both genetic backgrounds, but the tight hexagonal packing nearer the poles of anaphase B spindles was not observed in cdc25.22 mutant cells, where a more variable transverse architecture was present.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on comparison of wild-type and cdc25.22 spindles.

claim: Tight hexagonal packing nearer the poles of anaphase B spindles was not observed in cdc25.22 mutant cells.
source: Square packing is present at the midzone of anaphase B spindles in both genetic backgrounds, but the tight hexagonal packing nearer the poles of anaphase B spindles was not observed in cdc25.22 mutant cells, where a more variable transverse architecture was present.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on comparison of wild-type and cdc25.22 spindles.

claim: A beam will remain straight if subjected to forces below a critical threshold but will buckle if the critical force is exceeded.
source: The mechanical response of slender elastic beams under compression can be described using the Euler-Bernoulli beam theory (Landau and Lifshitz, 1986), which states that a beam will remain straight if subjected to forces below a certain threshold but will buckle if the critical force is exceeded.
evidence: This is stated in the results with a citation to beam theory.

claim: The critical force depends on the length of the beam, the elastic properties of the constituent material, and the beam's cross-section.
source: The critical force depends on the length of the beam, the elastic properties of the constituent material (specifically, its Young's modulus, E) and the beam's cross-section (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 2 and beam theory.

claim: Under purely compressive forces, beams with a constant cross-section will typically buckle in the direction of the most compliant principal axis.
source: However, under purely compressive forces beams with a constant cross-section will typically buckle in the direction of the most compliant principal axis (Figure 2E), and thus the minimal transverse stiffness, Imin, determines the critical force for beams of this type.
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 2E and beam theory.

claim: The minimal transverse stiffness contains peaks corresponding to specific microtubule numbers and organisations.
source: This analysis shows that the beam's minimal transverse stiffness contains peaks corresponding to specific microtubule numbers and organisations (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by analysis shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Removing a single microtubule from the 2 × 2 square motif reduces the minimal transverse stiffness by ∼1100%.
source: For example, removing a single microtubule from the 2 × 2 square motif in Figure 3D reduces the minimal transverse stiffness by ∼1100% while the addition of a further microtubule only gives rise to an increase of ∼3%.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by calculations shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Large increases in the minimal stiffness correspond to mechanically isotropic organisations, where Imin = Imax.
source: These large increases in the minimal stiffness correspond to mechanically isotropic organisations, where Imin = Imax.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on stiffness calculations.

claim: Peaks in the minimal transverse stiffness are present irrespective of the cross-linker density.
source: This analysis confirms that peaks in the minimal transverse stiffness are present irrespective of the cross-linker density, and are therefore associated with the geometry of square and hexagonal arrays (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The mean stiffness increases more rapidly for square-packed than for hexagonal bundles.
source: A notable feature of the stiffness of the idealised arrays, shown in Figure 3C,D, is that the mean stiffness increases more rapidly for the square-packed than for the hexagonal bundles.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Four hexagonally-packed microtubules have a mean stiffness of ∼21EIMT compared with the 2 × 2 motif's stiffness of ∼34EIMT.
source: This leads, for example, to four hexagonally-packed microtubules having a mean stiffness of ∼21EIMT compared with the 2 × 2 motif's stiffness of ∼34EIMT.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on stiffness calculations.

claim: The intrinsically higher hexagonal packing density is 2/√3 times greater than equivalent square packing.
source: This effect has two causes with the first being the intrinsically higher hexagonal packing density, which is 2/√3 times greater than equivalent square packing.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on geometric analysis.

claim: The square-packed architecture, larger number of microtubules, and increased bridging distance at the spindle midzone result in greater transverse stiffness than in the polar regions for all phases of spindle elongation.
source: We also observed that the square-packed architecture, larger number of microtubules and increased bridging distance between cross-linked microtubules at the spindle midzone result in a greater transverse stiffness than in the polar regions for all phases of spindle elongation (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: All anaphase B spindles have low mechanical anisotropy throughout their extent apart from localised stretches.
source: The estimates of the spindle's transverse anisotropy ratio reveal that all of the anaphase B spindles have low mechanical anisotropy throughout their extent apart from localised stretches (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Regions of high anisotropy may be associated with local loss of cross-linker integrity in early anaphase B spindles.
source: These regions may be associated with local loss of cross-linker integrity in early anaphase B spindles, where recruitment of anaphase-specific microtubule bundling factors is likely to be incomplete, and at the transitions from square to hexagonal microtubule packing arrangements in later spindles (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: This is stated in the results as a possible explanation, supported by data shown in Figure 3G,H.

claim: Anaphase B spindles from cdc25.22 mutant fission yeast cells and budding yeast contain similar structural microtubule motifs.
source: Remarkably, inspection of anaphase B spindles from cdc25.22 mutant fission yeast cells (Ding et al., 1993) and budding yeast (Winey et al., 1995) indicate that they also contain similar structural microtubule motifs.
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations to previous studies.

claim: The enlarged cytoplasmic volumes and greater polymer mass in cdc25.22 cells leads to spindles that retain nine microtubules at the spindle midzone in a 3 × 3 configuration late into anaphase B.
source: The enlarged cytoplasmic volumes and greater polymer mass in cdc25.22 cells (Ding et al., 1993) leads to spindles that retain the nine microtubules at the spindle midzone in a 3 × 3 configuration late into anaphase B.
evidence: This is stated in the results with a citation to previous work.

claim: Late anaphase B spindles in budding yeast contain around 20 μm of polymer and are often arranged with two long microtubules emanating from each pole.
source: Conversely, late anaphase B spindles in budding yeast contain around 20 μm of polymer, and are often arranged with two long microtubules emanating from each pole (Winey et al., 1995), and a 2 × 2 square-packed array in the central spindle.
evidence: This is stated in the results with a citation to previous work.

claim: The mechanisms of spindle assembly that give rise to mechanically isotropic arrangements are conserved in other yeast species.
source: This suggests that the mechanisms of spindle assembly that give rise to mechanically isotropic arrangements are conserved in other yeast species, and are adaptable to the increased abundance of tubulin in enlarged fission yeast cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a suggestion based on comparison of different yeast species.

claim: The critical force of the spindle decreases with spindle length.
source: The responses from computational models of wild-type spindles, compressed at the same rate (Figure 4D), shows that the critical force decreases with spindle length.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by computational simulations shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The critical force scales as Fc ∝ Ls−4 with spindle length.
source: A comparison of the critical forces for all of the simulations of ET-reconstructed spindles shows that it scales as Fc ∝ Ls−4 with spindle length (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by simulation data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The fourth-order dependence has a contribution from the beam theory, Fc ∝ EIeffLs−2, and another contribution from the conserved polymer mass.
source: This fourth-order dependence has a contribution from the beam theory, Fc ∝ EIeffLs−2, and another contribution from the conserved polymer mass (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on analysis of simulation data and beam theory.

claim: The polymer mass conservation gives rise to a quadratic decay in the spindles' effective transverse stiffness (EIeff ∝ Ls−2).
source: The polymer mass conservation gives rise to a quadratic decay in the spindles' effective transverse stiffness (EIeff ∝ Ls−2, see 'Materials and Methods').
evidence: This is stated in the results based on analysis of polymer mass conservation.

claim: The combination of a pushing mode of force generation with recycling of tubulin subunits and telescopic extension severely limits the forces that can be generated by a spindle architecture of this type.
source: This adverse scaling law suggests that the combination of a pushing mode of force generation with recycling of tubulin subunits and telescopic extension acts to severely limit the forces that can be generated by a spindle architecture of this type.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion based on the scaling law.

claim: Wild-type fission yeast spindles are substantially stronger than the random model.
source: This comparison reveals that the wild-type fission yeast spindles are substantially stronger than the random model (Figure 4F); a property that also applies to the cdc25.22 and the majority of budding yeast spindles (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by comparison data shown in Figure 4F and supplementary figures.

claim: Alternative spindle architectures with a larger critical force occur infrequently under the null model.
source: This analysis also indicates that alternative spindle architectures with a larger critical force occur infrequently under this null model, and suggests that the lengths of wild-type microtubules are regulated to increase the spindle's effective stiffness.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on comparison with the null model.

claim: Microtubules that are too short to reach the midzone cannot form associations with a partner from the opposing SPB.
source: In spindles where anti-parallel cross-linkers are confined to a region at the spindle centre, microtubules that are too short to reach the midzone cannot form associations with a partner from the opposing SPB (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and illustrated in Figure 5A.

claim: Maximally efficient overlap at the spindle midzone can be achieved by ensuring that all microtubules terminate at the furthest edge of the midzone and have a uniform length, LMT = (Ls + Lm)/2.
source: Maximally efficient overlap at the spindle midzone can thus be achieved by ensuring that all microtubules terminate at the furthest edge of the midzone, and have a uniform length, LMT = (Ls + Lm)/2, where Ls is the spindle length, and Lm the length of the overlap (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and illustrated in Figure 5B.

claim: Critical forces for MMO spindles are, on average, only 8% higher than those measured for reconstructed wild-type and cdc25.22 spindles.
source: Simulations probing the force-response of MMO spindles reveal critical forces that are, on average, only 8% higher than those measured for reconstructed wild-type and cdc25.22 spindles (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by simulation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Fission yeast cells exert precise global control on microtubule number and length.
source: This suggests that fission yeast cells exert precise global control on microtubule number and length.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion based on comparison with the MMO model.

claim: Microtubule numbers are under precise control in fission yeast.
source: A comparison of the observed number of interpolar microtubules in wild-type spindles, Nobs, with the theoretical prediction from equation 1 (Figure 5C, blue curve) confirms that microtubule numbers are under precise control in fission yeast.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by comparison data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The 2 × 2 motif can be maintained throughout spindle elongation up to lengths of around 10 μm.
source: The 2 × 2 motif can also be maintained throughout spindle elongation up to lengths of around 10 μm (Figure 5C), which coincides with the length at which GFP-tubulin spindles are observed to begin disassembly (Figure 1A; Videos 1, 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 1A.

claim: The theoretical curve for microtubule number in cdc25.22 spindles is in very close agreement with observed number of interpolar microtubules.
source: Remarkably, the theoretical curve for microtubule number in cdc25.22 spindles containing around twice the mass of polymerised tubulin (Figure 5C, red curve), is also in very close agreement with observed number of interpolar microtubules.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: All but four of the fourteen spindles deviate from the theoretical model by less than a single microtubule.
source: A direct comparison between Nobs and NMMO for wild-type and cdc25.22 spindles (Figure 5D) reveals that all but four of the fourteen spindles deviate from the theoretical model by less than a single microtubule, thus indicating precise scaling of microtubule number to changes in spindle length and the availability of polymerised tubulin.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by comparison data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The critical force of the longer spindles, at around 10 pN, is relatively small compared with other intracellular forces.
source: Whilst microtubule number and length appear to be regulated precisely in the fission yeast spindle, the critical force of the longer spindles, at around 10 pN (Figure 4E,F), is relatively small compared with other intracellular forces.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on simulation data shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: The critical force of longer spindles is comparable to the force generated by two kinesin motors.
source: For example, whilst this force exceeds the viscous drag on daughter nuclei in wild-type cells (see 'Materials and methods') it is comparable to the force generated by two kinesin motors (Gittes et al., 1996; Visscher et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations to kinesin force measurements.

claim: Exceeding the critical forces leads to the spindle being buckled into a shape with a single maximum (primary-mode buckling).
source: In simulations of the spindle, exceeding the critical forces leads to the spindle being buckled into a shape with a single maximum, which we refer to as primary-mode buckling (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: Laterally reinforcing microtubules with a dense elastic meshwork can lead to stable buckling over much shorter wavelengths.
source: It has, however, been shown, using experiments on cells and macroscopic analogues (Brangwynne et al., 2006), that laterally reinforcing microtubules with a dense elastic meshwork can lead to stable buckling over much shorter wavelengths.
evidence: This is stated in the results with a citation to previous work.

claim: The spindle's profile transitions from buckling in the primary mode when unreinforced to second-order buckling for an elastic confinement α = 40 Pa.
source: A visualisation of the shape adopted by the shortest anaphase B (Figure 6A) reveals that its profile transitions from buckling in the primary mode when unreinforced (α = 0) to second-order buckling for an elastic confinement α = 40 Pa, with intermediate configurations containing both components (α = 20 Pa).
evidence: This is stated in the results and illustrated in Figure 6A.

claim: The critical force that can be withstood increases with greater elastic confinement.
source: A comparison of the force-response curves for all of the simulated wild-type spindle architectures (Figure 6D) shows that the critical force that can be withstood increases with greater elastic confinement.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by simulation data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Large elastic confinements can increase the critical forces of the longest anaphase B spindles by around two orders of magnitude.
source: This effect is most dramatic for the longest anaphase B spindles where large elastic confinements can increase the critical forces by around two orders of magnitude.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on simulation data.

claim: The critical force of laterally reinforced spindles decreases much more slowly with increasing spindle length.
source: This effect is caused by the critical force of laterally reinforced spindles decreasing much more slowly with increasing spindle length (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: A small degree of lateral reinforcement could greatly increase the forces that the anaphase B spindle can sustain.
source: These results suggest that a small degree of lateral reinforcement, compared with the ∼1 kPa found in interphase mammalian cells (Brangwynne et al., 2006), could greatly increase the forces that the anaphase B spindle can sustain.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a suggestion based on simulation results.

claim: Yeast cells have evolved a spindle architecture that incorporates design principles similar to those used in man-made machines.
source: This study has shown that yeast cells have evolved a spindle architecture that incorporates similar design principles to those used in man-made machines.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion of the study.

claim: The relatively high abundance of midzone proteins and the force-resistant, non-slip binding of kinesin molecules to the microtubule lattice suggest that the spindle is densely cross-linked at the midzone.
source: In the case of the yeast spindle, the relatively high abundance of midzone proteins (Fu et al., 2009; Marguerat et al., 2012) and the force-resistant, non-slip binding of kinesin molecules to the microtubule lattice (Gittes et al., 1996; Visscher et al., 1999) suggest that the spindle is densely cross-linked at the midzone.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The dramatic remodelling of the spindle's transverse architecture at the boundary between the midzone and flanking regions suggests that the cross-linkers that bind to the polar regions also form rigid bridges between pairs of microtubules.
source: Furthermore, the dramatic remodelling of the spindle's transverse architecture at the boundary between the midzone and flanking regions of the spindle (Figure 3G,H) further suggests that the cross-linkers that bind to the polar regions also form rigid bridges between pairs of microtubules.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a suggestion based on observations shown in Figure 3G,H.

claim: The slow but uniform rate of spindle elongation suggests that the midzone-bound motors operate in a regime that is far from their stall force.
source: Finally, the slow but uniform rate of spindle elongation (Figure 1I) suggests that the midzone-bound motors operate in a regime that is far from their stall force.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a suggestion based on data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The key feature that endows the yeast spindle with rigidity is the crystalline microtubule architecture that is present throughout its extent.
source: The key feature that endows the yeast spindle with rigidity is the crystalline microtubule architecture that is present throughout its extent, and which takes the form of hexagonal packing in the polar regions of the spindle and square-packing at the spindle midzone.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: The advantage of crystals over more disordered microtubule packing arrangements is that the number of interactions between a microtubule and its neighbours is increased.
source: The advantage of crystals over more disordered microtubule packing arrangements is that the number of interactions between a microtubule and its neighbours is increased (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and illustrated in Figure 7A.

claim: Increased connectivity enhances the spindle's stiffness by ensuring that transverse rearrangements of microtubules that lead to bundle warping are prevented.
source: This increased connectivity enhances the spindle's stiffness by ensuring that transverse rearrangements of microtubules that lead to bundle warping are prevented, and that the structural integrity of the bundle is thus maintained.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an explanation for the advantage of crystalline packing.

claim: Arranging the crystalline units in each cross-section with rotational symmetry enhances the minimal transverse stiffness.
source: Arranging the crystalline units in each cross-section with rotational symmetry enhances the minimal transverse stiffness still further.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an explanation for the spindle's design.

claim: Dense, highly cross-linked, crystalline actin bundles in horseshoe sperm acrosomes are likely to have been selected for resistance to compressive forces.
source: Similar bundle design principles have also been observed in horseshoe sperm acrosomes, which are long, finger-like actin projections that enable the sperm cell to penetrate the 30 μm thick jelly coat that surrounds the egg (Schmid et al., 2004; Shin et al., 2004). These dense, highly cross-linked, crystalline actin bundles are likely to have been selected for resistance to compressive forces (Schmid et al., 2004), and the composite structure has a Young's modulus that is similar to that of the constituent actin filaments (Shin et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The convergent evolution of a crystalline architecture in cytoskeletal bundles that resist compressive forces may reflect the relative contributions of tensile and compressive forces in each system.
source: The convergent evolution of a crystalline architecture in cytoskeletal bundles that resist compressive forces may be one factor that has led to the distinct transverse arrangements that are observed in different populations of spindle microtubules (McDonald et al., 1979, 1992; Mastronarde et al., 1993) and may reflect the relative contributions of tensile and compressive forces in each system (Wühr et al., 2009; Goshima and Scholey, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a speculation with supporting citations.

claim: The regulation of microtubule length and number enables the fission yeast spindle to use the available microtubule polymer to form specific square-packed midzone motifs at critical points during mitosis.
source: We have provided evidence that the regulation of these properties enables the fission yeast spindle to use the available microtubule polymer to form specific square-packed midzone motifs at critical points during mitosis (Figure 1C; Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 5C.

claim: The regulation of spindle architecture is maintained in enlarged cdc25.22 cells.
source: A surprising feature of the spindle is that the regulation of its architecture is maintained in enlarged cdc25.22 cells.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on comparison of wild-type and cdc25.22 cells.

claim: The mechanisms of spindle assembly can adapt its morphology to changes in cell size.
source: This suggests that the mechanisms of spindle assembly can adapt its morphology to changes in cell size.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a suggestion based on observations in cdc25.22 cells.

claim: The maximal force that can be exerted on chromosomes in spermatocyte spindles is typically several orders of magnitude larger than that required to overcome viscous drag from the surrounding cytoplasm.
source: In studies of spermatocyte spindles and related systems (Nicklas, 1988), it was found that the maximal force that can be exerted on chromosomes is typically several orders of magnitude larger than that required to overcome viscous drag from the surrounding cytoplasm.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to previous work.

claim: The most long-lived kinetochore-microtubule attachments in budding yeast take place under loads of around 5 pN.
source: In vitro studies of purified budding yeast kinetochores (Akiyoshi et al., 2010) found that the tensile force exerted on a single microtubule influences the life-time of its association with the kinetochore. The most long-lived kinetochore-microtubule attachments take place under loads of around 5 pN, with weaker or stronger forces leading to increased rates of detachment (Akiyoshi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to in vitro studies.

claim: The total tensile force on the budding yeast spindle could be around 80 pN at the end of metaphase.
source: As the positions of the 16 kinetochore pairs in budding yeast are highly consistent during metaphase (Joglekar et al., 2009), when microtubule attachments are at their most long-lived (Tanaka, 2010), this suggests that the total tensile force on the budding yeast spindle could be around 80 pN at the end of metaphase.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a suggestion based on kinetochore properties and citations.

claim: Fission yeast spindles have complex centromeres with around three microtubules occupying each kinetochore.
source: Fission yeast spindles have complex centromeres, which more closely resemble those of higher eukaryotes (Malik and Henikoff, 2009), with around three microtubules occupying each kinetochore (Ding et al., 1993) compared with the single microtubule in budding yeast (Tanaka, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Extrapolating in vitro estimates from budding yeast to fission yeast would suggest a force in the range of ∼50 pN.
source: The coordination between microtubules within composite kinetochore-fibres is currently unknown but extrapolating the in vitro estimates from budding yeast to the three chromosomes in fission yeast would suggest a force in the range of ∼50 pN.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an extrapolation from budding yeast data.

claim: Shorter, stiffer metaphase spindles can easily generate the required forces without external mechanical reinforcement.
source: This value is well below the critical force of unsupported early anaphase spindles, and suggests that shorter, stiffer metaphase spindles (Figure 1C) can easily generate the required forces without external mechanical reinforcement.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a suggestion based on comparison of forces.

claim: In later anaphase B, the major external loads opposing spindle elongation are likely to arise from cytoplasmic resistance to the movement of daughter nuclei.
source: However, in later anaphase B, after the nuclear envelope splits into a 'dumb-bell' morphology, the major external loads opposing spindle elongation are likely to arise from cytoplasmic resistance to the movement of daughter nuclei (Lim et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: The final estimate for the total resistive force acting on the poles of the elongating spindle is of the same order of magnitude (∼1–10 pN) as the critical force of longer anaphase B spindles.
source: The final estimate for the total resistive force acting on the poles of the elongating spindle is subject to a large degree of uncertainty, but is of the same order of magnitude (∼1–10 pN) as the critical force of longer anaphase B spindles.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on calculations of viscous and elastic forces.

claim: The wild-type spindle can support the drag forces that resist its elongation under normal conditions.
source: This suggests that the wild-type spindle can support the drag forces that resist its elongation under normal conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a suggestion based on force estimates.

claim: The spindle may be subjected to larger forces if chromosomes are concatenated or are not properly bi-oriented in metaphase.
source: However, the spindle may be subjected to larger forces if chromosomes are concatenated or are not properly bi-oriented in metaphase (Pidoux et al., 2000; Courtheoux et al., 2009; Petrova et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The klp9p motors that bind to the spindle midzone could theoretically generate up to ∼103 pN.
source: Under increased loads, the klp9p motors that bind to the spindle midzone (Visscher et al., 1999; Fu et al., 2009; Marguerat et al., 2012) could theoretically generate up to ∼103 pN, while each depolymerising microtubule, of which there are around nine in fission yeast cells during anaphase A (Ding et al., 1993), can produce a maximal force of ∼40 pN (Grishchuk et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Each depolymerising microtubule can produce a maximal force of ∼40 pN.
source: Under increased loads, the klp9p motors that bind to the spindle midzone (Visscher et al., 1999; Fu et al., 2009; Marguerat et al., 2012) could theoretically generate up to ∼103 pN, while each depolymerising microtubule, of which there are around nine in fission yeast cells during anaphase A (Ding et al., 1993), can produce a maximal force of ∼40 pN (Grishchuk et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Candidates for providing mechanical support to the spindle include actin, the nuclear envelope, and mitotic chromosomes.
source: It remains to be determined whether the anaphase B spindle is reinforced, but candidates for providing this mechanical support have been identified and include actin, which is required for accurate chromosome segregation in fission yeast (Gachet et al., 2001; Meadows and Millar, 2008), the nuclear envelope (Lim et al., 2007; Yam et al., 2011) and mitotic chromosomes themselves, which surround the interpolar microtubule axis of yeast spindles (Stephens et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The architecture of the beam-like fission yeast spindle is sculpted for the generation of pushing forces.
source: Whilst this study has provided evidence that the architecture of the beam-like fission yeast spindle is sculpted for the generation of pushing forces, a more general question concerns why this linear morphology was selected in yeast cells compared with the more conventional ellipsoid spindles observed in metazoans and many other eukaryotes.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion of the study.

claim: Fungal cells have evolved a stiff polysaccharide cell wall that encloses the plasma membrane.
source: One possible functional explanation for the change in spindle morphology is that fungal cells have evolved a stiff polysaccharide cell wall that encloses the plasma membrane (Bowman and Free, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: The cell wall innovation could have reduced the cell's dependence on the cytoskeleton for providing motility and structural support.
source: This innovation could then have reduced the cell's dependence on the cytoskeleton for providing motility and structural support, and enabled reduced expression of the tubulin and actin isoforms (Pollard et al., 2000; Marguerat et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a speculation with supporting citations.

claim: In yeast cells with a small cytoplasmic volume, the beam-like spindle morphology may have been selected to segregate chromosomes with reduced use of structural components.
source: In yeast cells with a small cytoplasmic volume, the beam-like spindle morphology may have been selected to segregate chromosomes with reduced use of structural components and their associated metabolic cost to the cell.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a speculation.

claim: Chromosomes are transported over similar distances in yeast and many somatic mammalian cell types.
source: In this respect, the yeast spindle is indeed remarkably efficient, as chromosomes are transported over similar distances to those in many somatic mammalian cell types (Goshima and Scholey, 2010), but with a structure that has a 1000-fold smaller volume.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: The yeast spindle has a 1000-fold smaller volume than spindles in many somatic mammalian cell types.
source: In this respect, the yeast spindle is indeed remarkably efficient, as chromosomes are transported over similar distances to those in many somatic mammalian cell types (Goshima and Scholey, 2010), but with a structure that has a 1000-fold smaller volume.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on comparison of spindle volumes.

claim: Electron tomography has several advantages over the serial-section electron microscopy method.
source: In this study, we reconstruct the architecture of wild-type fission yeast spindles using electron tomography (ET) (Höög et al., 2007; Roque et al., 2010). This technique has several advantages (Soto et al., 1994) over the serial-section electron microscopy method that was used previously to determine the structures of spindles in cdc25.22 fission yeast and budding yeast cells (Ding et al., 1993; Winey et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The main disadvantage of serial-section electron microscopy is that movements of the microtubules perpendicular to the imaging plane cannot be fully accounted for.
source: The main disadvantage of this technique is that movements of the microtubules perpendicular to the imaging plane cannot be fully accounted for, which can cause straightening of microtubules during the registration step.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a limitation of serial-section EM.

claim: Serial-section EM provides accurate estimates of microtubule length and transverse organisation in linear microtubule bundles.
source: The technique provides accurate estimates of microtubule length and transverse organisation in linear microtubule bundles, but it may be impossible to track strongly curved microtubules, which, by definition, have an orientation that varies along their length.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a property of serial-section EM.

claim: Electron tomography largely overcomes the difficulties of serial-section EM by imaging the sample at numerous orientations.
source: These difficulties are largely overcome by electron tomography where the sample is imaged at numerous orientations (i.e. a tilt series) with respect to the imaging plane (Soto et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: Curvature in anaphase B spindles appears to be inconsistent with the linear spindle morphology observed via light microscopy.
source: An interesting feature of the tomographic spindle reconstructions of wild-type cells is the curvature that is present in all of the anaphase B spindles (Figure 1B). These deflections are more pronounced in the early anaphase B spindles, where they appear to be inconsistent with the linear spindle morphology that can be observed in cells via light microscopy (Mallavarapu et al., 1999; Tolić-Nørrelykke, Sacconi, et al., 2004b; Khodjakov et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations to light microscopy studies.

claim: The deflections in spindles are caused partially or entirely by the standard preparation methods for electron tomography.
source: This suggests that the deflections are caused partially or entirely by the standard preparation methods for electron tomography (Giddings et al., 2001; Höög and Antony, 2007; Buser, 2010), and that native spindles have a straighter morphology.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a suggestion with supporting citations.

claim: The IFTA algorithm was developed to trace the path of the spindle in three dimensions and computationally straighten the spindle.
source: In the absence of further confirmation of the degree of microtubule curvature in live cells; we developed the IFTA algorithm to trace the path of the spindle in three dimensions. This enabled us to computationally straighten the spindle, and to infer the microtubule arrangements in the plane perpendicular to the spindle's main axis, independently of any spindle curvature.
evidence: This is stated in the results describing the development of the IFTA algorithm.

claim: The spindle is highly symmetric from late metaphase onwards with an almost identical number of microtubules nucleated from each spindle pole.
source: In both genetic backgrounds, the spindle is highly symmetric from late metaphase onwards with an almost identical number of microtubules nucleated from each spindle pole (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The total length of tubulin polymerised in spindle microtubules remains constant throughout anaphase B in both wild-type and cdc25.22 conditions.
source: The total length of tubulin polymerised in spindle microtubules also appears to remain constant throughout anaphase B, in both conditions, which is accommodated by a gradual reduction in microtubule numbers.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on comparison of wild-type and cdc25.22 spindles.

claim: cdc25.22 spindles contain around twice the quantity of polymerised tubulin compared to wild-type spindles.
source: The most striking difference is that cdc25.22 spindles contain around twice the quantity of polymerised tubulin.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on comparison of wild-type and cdc25.22 spindles.

claim: The cdc25.22 allele is hypomorphic under permissive temperatures and causes cells to divide at lengths that are around twice that of wild-type cells.
source: The likely cause for this discrepancy is the cdc25.22 mutation, which causes the allele of the mitotic phosphatase cdc25p to be inactivated by high temperature (Russell and Nurse, 1986). The cdc25.22 allele is hypomorphic under the permissive temperatures used by Ding et al., and consequently cells divide at lengths that are around twice that of wild-type cells (Hagan et al., 1990).
evidence: This is stated in the results with supporting citations.
